mappings.note: Opening a torch and picking out the cells, lamp and switch is identifying components by what can be seen. Not LO-20, because nothing is tested or recorded; the torch is only examined.

The protruding cap, the flat disc and the plus and minus marks are the observable features by which a cell's terminals are told apart. Not LO-18, since one object is being described rather than two being differentiated.

Whether the lamp glows depends on the cells being seated positive to negative, so the outcome is tied to its cause. Not LO-17, because the arrangement, not the appearance of the cell, decides the answer.
Inspecting how the filament is held and where each support wire runs to the base contact and the metal casing is identification of a component by its visible structure.
Sets an LED against an incandescent lamp: no filament, and terminals told apart by lead length. That contrast of two devices by their structure is LO-18, not LO-17.
Six cell-and-lamp arrangements to predict, try and record in a table is the conduct-and-record investigation outcome. Not LO-21, because the item asks for observations rather than an explanation.

Reversing the LED leads stops it glowing because current passes one way only; the observation is tied to its cause. Not LO-20, since the point of the step is the conclusion about polarity, not the recording.

Building a working switch from drawing pins, a safety pin and wire is constructing a device from materials at hand and explaining how it works. Not LO-31, because the design is prescribed rather than invented.

Explains the ON and OFF positions in terms of a closed path carrying current and an open gap stopping it. Explanation of the process, so LO-22 rather than LO-27, which covered the building of the switch.

The tester is used object by object and the results recorded (LO-20), then each material is labelled conductor or insulator (LO-18, which names conductors and insulators explicitly). Both halves are assessed.

The false statement is that a switch is the source of current, so the item turns on understanding what a switch does in a circuit and what actually drives the current. Not LO-17, because a role in the circuit, not an observable feature, is being tested.
Choosing what to place at the gap so the lamp stays dark is exactly differentiating insulators from conductors, the example named in LO-18.

One broken filament stops the other lamp because a series loop offers a single path; the effect is traced to its cause. Not LO-22, since the item does not describe the current's effect, only why the path fails.

The lamp stays dark because the insulation was left on the wire ends: the failure is traced to its cause. LO-18 is the underlying knowledge, but the item asks for the consequence, not for a material to be sorted.
Draws a torch circuit using standard component symbols, and LO-25 names electric circuits among the diagrams to be drawn.
Works out which lamps glow for four combinations of two switches, relating each outcome to the state of the circuit. Not LO-25, because the diagram is supplied and nothing is drawn.

Lists possible faults and then asks what the student would do to find the real one, which is planning an investigation. Not LO-21, because no single cause is given to explain; the item is about how to hunt for one.
Picks out the cases in which a closed switch still leaves the lamp dark, tying each failure to its cause in the circuit.

Suggesting a way to find the terminals of an unmarked battery, for instance with an LED of known polarity, is devising a test. Not LO-17, because the markings that identification would rely on are precisely what is missing.
Carrying out the activity that sorts working cells from dead ones is a simple investigation with recorded results.
First judge why Tanya's cells will not light the LED (LO-21, the series rule), then redraw the wires correctly (LO-25, drawing the circuit). Both are required by the question.
How a hydroelectric power house at Bhakra Nangal makes electricity is an account of a process. Not LO-30, because no protective or conservation action is asked of the student.
Placing a room heater in the heating and cooling group of electrical uses is classification by function. Not LO-18, since a category is being populated rather than two things told apart.
Why school experiments must use cells and never the mains is everyday electrical safety, the day-to-day application outcome. Not LO-32, because the concern is danger, not honesty or objectivity.

Names the parts found inside a torch. First of a cluster of component-recall items in this batch that the frame houses only in LO-17, since each asks what a part is or where it is, not how two parts differ.
Terminals as the name for a cell's two connection points: identification of a part.
The protruding metal cap as the positive terminal, identified by its appearance.
The flat metal disc as the negative terminal, the companion identification to the cap item.
The cell as a portable source of electrical energy is identification by function, which C-SCI1.1 lists alongside appearance and texture.
Naming a battery as two or more connected cells. Still component vocabulary, so it stays with the identification cluster rather than LO-21, where the connection rule itself is tested.
The positive-to-negative series rule is what makes the device work, so the arrangement is tied to the outcome. Unlike the battery-definition item, here the rule rather than the name carries the mark.
Why reversing one cell kills the torch: the failure is traced to the broken positive-to-negative sequence.
Naming the filament inside the bulb, identification of a visible part.
Counting the lamp's two terminals: again identification of the component's contacts.
Asks explicitly for the difference between an LED and an incandescent lamp, so LO-18 rather than LO-17; two devices are set against each other.
The longer lead marks the positive terminal of an LED, an identification made from an observable feature. Not LO-18, because only the LED is in view.

The lamp glows only when an unbroken path links the cell's terminals through it: explanation of why current flows and lights the lamp. Not LO-21, since the item states the general condition rather than diagnosing one case.
Defines the electrical circuit as the closed path for current, the central process idea of the chapter. Not LO-25, because nothing is drawn.
The conventional direction of current, positive to negative, is part of explaining how current is described in a circuit. Not LO-25, because the convention is stated, not used to draw a diagram.
A fused lamp means a broken filament, and therefore an open circuit: the symptom is traced to its cause. Not LO-17, because the break is not something the item asks the student to see.
